question: Two weeks after undergoing an emergency cardiac catheterization for unstable angina pectoris, a 65-year-old man has decreased urinary output. He takes naproxen for osteoarthritis and was started on aspirin, clopidogrel, and metoprolol after the coronary intervention. His temperature is 38.1°C (100.5°F), pulse is 96/min, and blood pressure is 128/88 mm Hg. Examination shows mottled, reticulated purplish discoloration of the feet and ischemic changes on the right big toe. His leukocyte count is 16,500/mm3 with 56% segmented neutrophils, 12% eosinophils, 30% lymphocytes, and 2% monocytes. His serum creatinine concentration is 4.5 mg/dL. A photomicrograph of a kidney biopsy specimen is shown. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's presentation?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Emergency cardiac catheterization" -> "release of cholesterol crystals" -> "cholesterol embolization" -> "mottled purplish discoloration of feet" -> "ischemic changes on toe" -> "elevated serum creatinine" -> "decreased urinary output" -> 95%
CHAIN: "Naproxen use" -> "decreased renal perfusion" -> "contrast-induced nephropathy" -> "elevated serum creatinine" -> "decreased urinary output" -> "possible" -> 60%
CHAIN: "Aspirin and clopidogrel use" -> "increased bleeding risk" -> "possible renal impairment" -> "elevated serum creatinine" -> "decreased urinary output" -> "unclear" -> 50%
CHAIN: "Recent cardiac catheterization" -> "contrast exposure" -> "contrast-induced nephropathy" -> "elevated serum creatinine" -> "decreased urinary output" -> "possible" -> 65%
CHAIN: "Naproxen use" -> "allergic interstitial nephritis" -> "elevated eosinophils" -> "elevated serum creatinine" -> "decreased urinary output" -> "possible" -> 55%
analysis: The patient presents with decreased urinary output, fever, elevated serum creatinine, and a high eosinophil count following a cardiac catheterization. The mottled, reticulated purplish discoloration of the feet and ischemic changes on the toe suggest peripheral embolization. These findings, along with the recent invasive procedure, are consistent with cholesterol embolization syndrome. This condition is characterized by the release of cholesterol crystals from atherosclerotic plaques, which can occur after vascular interventions, leading to renal impairment and skin changes. The presence of eosinophilia further supports this diagnosis.
